>change you proposed here will tick the rate once for each queue, and hence give erroneous results if there are more than one.

oh yes, there's a hardcoded assumption that the `tick()` will only be called once per `shardUpdateDuration`. I think we can do away with this limitation. Calling `tick()` more often on `samplesIn` will allow us to be more reactive to the changes in flow and hence not allow the backlog to build a lot...

issue_context.title: Stop remote-write flapping between two shard counts
issue_context.body:
I took this screen grab to illustrate: shards is flapping from 2 to 3 and back again, as the lag between queued data and sent data grows and falls.  Round-trip latency is broadly flat over the period.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/8125524/129541393-fd6f0899-d937-43d4-a722-a68334bd2445.png)

I see that when desired-shards moves from 2.01 to 1.99 this triggers an instant shard-down from 3 to 2, only to see lag increase and shard back up to 3 again.

The algorithm avoids shifts of less than 30%, however 3->2 is 33% (and 2->1 is 50%).
One simple modification would be to also prohibit a downshard of 1.

I considered adding more dampening to the algorithm, but in my picture it's happening over 20-40 minutes; it's hard to imagine dampening that works a bit better at that scale but doesn't still oscillate over hours.
comments: The only problem could be when users have set queue configs that will result in them only ever needing a small amount of shards, and where sharding up or down by one shard changes throughput a lot.
Going _up_ by one would be allowed.
Hello from the bug scrub: no new development in 3 years, closing. Please reopen if there's new information or volunteering with a PR.

review_comments: The units here no longer make sense, `integralGain` has units of `1/seconds` so if multiplied by a rate we are now trying to add `1/seconds` and `1/seconds^2`.

https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/752c4f11ae86effa9a46f017f2feb66730c67ed8/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L830

hmm, cmiiw `integralGain` has no units (`const * T/T` => `const * const`)

Though I found another issue in `dataOutDuration` which I have now fixed.
Hmm... I could also be wrong. I think `integralGain` is `const / (nanoseconds/(nanoseconds/seconds)) => const / seconds` right now though?

>I think integralGain is const / (nanoseconds/(nanoseconds/seconds)) => const / seconds right now

why does `time.Second` have units `(nanoseconds/seconds)`? 🤔 

here's what I have in my head:

```
| var             | formula                                        | dimensions                                     |
|-----------------+------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------|
| dataInRate      | rate of samples ingested per sec               | samples/T                                      |
| dataOutRate     | rate of samples output per sec                 | samples/T                                      |
| dataDroppedRate | rate of samples dropped per sec                | samples/T                                      |
| dataOutDuration | rate of time spent on each send per sec        | T/T => const                                   |
| dataKeptRatio   | 1 - (dataDroppedRate / dataInRate)             | 1 - (samples/T) / (samples/T) => const         |
| dataPendingRate | dataInRate - dataOutRate - dataDroppedRate     | samples/T - samples/T - samples/T => samples/T |
| integralGain    | 0.5 / float64(shardUpdateDuration/time.Second) | const / (T/T) => const                         |
| timePerSample   | dataOutDuration / dataOutRate                  | const / (samples/T) => T/samples               |
```

Thus, we get `desiredShards` which has the formula:

`timePerSample * (dataInRate*dataKeptRatio + integralGain*dataPendingRate)` become:

```
T/samples * (samples/T * const + const * samples/T)
T/samples * (samples/T)
const
```
It is because any `time.Duration` in Go is stored in nanoseconds. `time.Second` is then used to convert from nanoseconds to seconds to be in the same unit as all the other rates we have.

> > why does time.Second have units (nanoseconds/seconds)? 🤔

> It is because any time.Duration in Go is stored in nanoseconds. time.Second is then used to convert from nanoseconds to seconds to be in the same unit as all the other rates we have.

Conversion from nanosecond -> seconds shouldn't change the units since it's just division by a const (`1e9`). 
`time.Second` should have dimension `T` still, isn't it?
https://github.com/golang/go/blob/1d91551b7326383343c7c143a8ac299d0a685289/src/time/time.go#L608-L612
